","createdAt":"2026-08-11T06:20:54Z","labels":[],"number":127,"title":"CMakeLists' tournament timing comment is wrong in all three of its claims","updatedAt":"2026-08-11T06:20:54Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/127"},{"assignees":[],"body":"`check_section()` in `tests/instructions.sh` asks for the section heading and
for **one** quoted mention of the section name somewhere above it. Its failure
message for the new `Who runs which tests` section, however, says:

> steps 4 and 7 point at it

Both really do today (`AGENTS.md:152` and `AGENTS.md:229`). Delete either one
and the test stays green while the message's claim stops being true — verified
both ways by the `verifier`: with only step 4's pointer the script exits 0, and
with only step 7's it exits 0.

## Why it matters

The section is reached from two different steps because they do two different
things with it — step 4 is told not to delegate its loop, step 7 is told the
battery is its own work. Losing either pointer loses that step's reader, and
nothing notices. This is a check that asserts less than its own error message
claims, which is the shape AGENTS.md step 9 asks to be filed.

The same is true of `Answering a finding`, which steps 6, 7 and 8 all state and
which one surviving mention satisfies. It is only sharper for the new section
because its message names the two steps.

## How to see it

```sh
python3 - <<'PY'
import re
t = open('AGENTS.md').read()
open('/tmp/a/AGENTS.md','w').write(re.sub(r'"Who runs which\s+tests" after this list says why', 'it says why', t))
PY
cp CLAUDE.md /tmp/a/ && sh tests/instructions.sh /tmp/a    # exits 0, step 4's pointer gone
```

Note the newline-aware replacement: step 4's pointer wraps mid-phrase, so a
line-wise `sed` cannot remove it. `tests/instructions.sh` carries a comment
about that, since it is how the first mutation attempt against this check came
back green for the wrong reason.

## Fix sketch

Counting pointers rather than finding one would catch it, at the cost of a
number to maintain per section — the same trade `STANDARDS` already makes a few
lines above, and with the same failure mode when someone rewords legitimately.
The stronger fix is the one #65 and #105 are circling: attribute a pointer to
the step it sits in, so the check can say "step 4 no longer points at this"
rather than "nothing does". None of the three can be done well without that
attribution, so this may belong to #65 rather than to a fix of its own.

## Provenance

Reported by the `verifier` as missing coverage while verifying the change that
added the section. Filed rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9.
","createdAt":"2026-08-11T05:36:25Z","labels":[],"number":126,"title":"instructions.sh accepts one pointer where its message claims two","updatedAt":"2026-08-11T05:36:25Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/126"},{"assignees":[],"body":"The message window's depth is derived from two constants:

- `PANELH` is 13 (`tui.c:15`)
- `msgh = LINES-PANELH > 1 ? LINES-PANELH : 1` (`tui.c:202`)
- `tui_pageheight() = LINES-PANELH-1` (`tui.c:987`)

Which gives a three-step progression as the terminal gets shorter:

- **fifteen rows** — two message rows, one of which is the pager, so output
  arrives a line at a time
- **fourteen rows** — one message row, and `tui_pageheight()` is 0, so the
  pager takes the only line there is and a scan pages past without showing
  any of itself (this is the state #95 is about)
- **thirteen rows** — the message window starts at row `PANELH`, which is off
  a thirteen-row screen, so there is no conversation and no prompt anywhere
  (this is #94)
- **shorter** — `panelh = LINES` and the panels themselves start losing rows
  off the bottom

`tests/tui.sh` visits fourteen and eleven rows (`tests/tui.sh:1079`, `:1391`,
`:1507-1524`) but asserts panel geometry and prompt survival there, not this
progression. Nothing ties the numbers to the behaviour.

## Why it matters

`sst.doc` now states all three thresholds by name, as of the change for #113 —
"at fifteen rows it arrives a line at a time, at fourteen the pager takes the
only line there is and a scan pages past without showing any of itself, and at
thirteen there is none of it left at all". Those are the numbers a player uses
to decide whether the window they are looking at is broken or merely small.

Change `PANELH`, or the `-1` in `tui_pageheight()`, or the `> 1` guard on
`msgh`, and every one of those sentences becomes wrong while the whole suite
stays green. The manual is currently the only thing in the repository that
records the progression, and it is the one thing nothing checks.

## How to see it

```sh
tmux -f /dev/null -L t new-session -d -x 80 -y 15 -s s './build/sst -t; sleep 30'
```

Drive a game to the command prompt, run `srscan`, and count how much arrives
per `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]`. Repeat at `-y 14` (nothing but the pager
prompt) and `-y 13` (no prompt at all).

## Fix sketch

A block in `tests/tui.sh` alongside the existing sub-minimum coverage: at
fifteen rows assert one content line per pager stop; at fourteen assert the
single message row holds only the pager prompt and that the scan's first line
never appears; at thirteen assert no prompt is on screen and the panels'
bottom border is. Each of those can be broken by changing `PANELH` or
`tui_pageheight()`, which is the failing-first-run proof AGENTS.md step 4
asks for on a test written against behaviour that already exists.

## Provenance

Reported by the `verifier` while verifying #113, as coverage missing for code
the change did not touch. Filed rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9.
Related: #94 and #95 record the fourteen- and thirteen-row states themselves;
this is about nothing testing them.
","createdAt":"2026-08-11T04:54:07Z","labels":[],"number":123,"title":"Nothing ties the 15/14/13-row message-window thresholds to their behaviour","updatedAt":"2026-08-11T04:54:07Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/123"},{"assignees":[],"body":"`README.md`'s "Full-screen mode" section promises more than the game does,
and then contradicts itself forty lines later.

## The over-promise

`README.md:19-21`:

> both the question you were asked and the answer you were halfway through
> typing survive, **so long as there is still room for them**

The room is not the condition. `restore_curline()` (`tui.c:402`) restores a
part-typed answer only when `curline` is non-empty — a prompt written with
`proutn`, which has not ended its line. A prompt written with `prout` ends its
own line, so `curlen` is 0 by the time the reader waits, and the function
takes its `curlen == 0` branch and returns at `tui.c:436` the moment
`pending_answer` is non-empty. Nothing is restored, however much room there
is.

Reproduced by `ui-review` at 80x24 with plenty of room to spare: the warp-time
question (`moving.c:594`, a `prout`), `y` typed and not entered, squeezed to
80x14. The surviving conversation row came back reading `Helmsman Sulu- "Warp
factor 1.0, Captain."` — old conversation — with the reader still holding the
invisible `y`.

`README.md:53-56` describes this correctly ("The one gap left is a question
you have already started answering"). So the file is internally inconsistent,
and the reassuring sentence is the one a player reads first.

Worth fixing together with the related correction now on #117: in that state a
resize loses *both* the question and the answer, not just the question.

## The over-generalization

`README.md:71-72`:

> answer `N` there and you are back at the prompt, free to give the command
> again

Not always. At `Do you want to play again?` (`sst.c:507-508`) `N` ends the
session, and there is no command to give again. The same sentence was written
into `sst.doc` for #113 and taken out again after `ui-review` raised it; the
manual now says only "answer N to decline whatever it was".

## Trivial

`README.md:42-43` lists the free readings as `srscan`, `status`, `chart`,
`damages`. `LRSCAN` is equally free and is the one that helps a player who has
lost sight of where they are; `sst.doc` now names it.

## Provenance

Found by `ui-review` while reviewing #113, which corrected the same two claims
in `sst.doc`. `README.md` is outside that slice, so filed rather than fixed,
per AGENTS.md step 9.
","createdAt":"2026-08-11T04:24:01Z","labels":[],"number":122,"title":"README's resize section over-promises, then contradicts itself","updatedAt":"2026-08-15T18:10:17Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/122"},{"assignees":[],"body":"`sst.doc` is paginated with form feeds, and each page carries its number in
the heading line that follows the break. Measured between form feeds, the
pages run 47 to 67 lines — except `MODIFICATIONS` (page 26, `sst.doc:1471`),
which was already 81 lines and is 125 after the change for #113.

## Why it matters

Anyone printing or paging the manual gets one physical sheet per form feed.
Page 26 is now close to two of them, so the number printed at the top stops
agreeing with the sheet you are holding, and the page numbers in the table of
contents (`sst.doc:54-77`) stop being a way to find anything after it.

It is also a trap for the next person adding to the `-t` documentation, which
is where the growth is coming from: the section has no natural stopping point
and nothing signals that it has outgrown its page.

## How to see it

```sh
awk '/\f/{if (prev) printf "%d lines before the break at %d\n", NR-prev, NR; prev=NR}' sst.doc
```

The last three figures are 55, 67 and 125. Every other page in the file is
inside the 47-67 band.

## Fix sketch

Split `MODIFICATIONS` across two pages with a form feed and a `26 (cont.)`
style heading, or renumber from 26 onward — the latter also touches the table
of contents, since `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS` and `REFERENCES` follow. Renumbering is
the tidier result and the larger diff.

Worth deciding first whether the pagination is load-bearing at all: nothing in
the game reads it (`helpme()` skips form feeds outright, `sst.c:180`), and its
last help topic is at `sst.doc:1294`, well before this page. If the answer is
that nobody prints the manual, the honest fix may be to say so and stop
maintaining the numbers.

## Provenance

Found by `ui-review` while reviewing #113, as a nit against a change that
makes it worse without causing it. Filed rather than fixed there, per
AGENTS.md step 9.
","createdAt":"2026-08-11T03:52:49Z","labels":[],"number":121,"title":"MODIFICATIONS has outgrown its page number in sst.doc","updatedAt":"2026-08-11T04:24:30Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/121"},{"assignees":[],"body":"`helpme()` (`sst.c:127-199`) is the only thing that opens `sst.doc`, and it
prints exactly one shape of entry. It builds a key of `  Mnemonic:  <COMMAND>`
— or ` ABBREV` for the abbreviation table — scans forward for the first line
carrying that prefix, and prints until a line containing `******`.

So the only text `help` can reach is a command entry. The last one is
`  Mnemonic:  SCORE` at `sst.doc:1294`, and the `ABBREV` table is at
`sst.doc:1406`. Everything after that is unreachable from inside the game:

- `MISCELLANEOUS NOTES` (1302) — black holes, the Neutral Zone, ramming
  commanders, how fast the Super-commander travels
- `SCORING` (1349) — the whole scoring table
- `MODIFICATIONS` (1471), which includes the full-screen `-t` section at
  1541 and everything #113 is adding to it
- `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS` (1552) and `REFERENCES` (1573)

## Why it matters

The game names `sst.doc` to the player and refuses to give help without it
("You need to find SST.DOC and put it in the current directory", `sst.c:163`),
which reads as a promise that the file is the manual the game will show you.
It shows you a fifth of it. A player who wants to know what the scoring
actually is, or what happens when they drag the window, has to leave the game
and open the file in a pager.

This is what makes #113's premise only half true — the manual is the right
home for that text, but adding it there does not put it in front of a player
mid-game.

## How to see it

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug && cmake --build build
printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nhelp score\n' | ./build/sst
```

`help score` prints the `SCORE` *command* entry (`sst.doc:1294`), not the
`SCORING` section (1349). There is no argument at all that reaches 1541.

## Fix sketch

`help` would need a way to name a topic that is not a command. Either a
second key shape in `helpme()` — a `  Topic:  <NAME>` line placed above the
narrative sections, terminated the same way — or a `help display` /
`help scoring` special-cased the way ` ABBREV` already is at `sst.c:152-154`.

Found while doing #113, checking the claim that `sst.doc` is what a player
reaches from inside the game. Filed rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md
step 9.
","createdAt":"2026-08-11T03:39:12Z","labels":[],"number":120,"title":"Most of sst.doc is unreachable from in-game help","updatedAt":"2026-08-17T18:33:02Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/120"},{"assignees":[],"body":"The `a wrapping answer survives a grow` block in `tests/tui.sh` counts the
question and stops there. The answer — the half the player is actually looking
at — is unchecked, so a change that lost it, doubled it, or left the cursor
behind it would pass.

The question assertion alone does kill the mutant the block exists for (cutting
`restore_curline()`'s joined-row search back to one row), so this is coverage
rather than a hole. But the answer is the part that *wraps*, which is the whole
reason the joined search exists, so it is the more direct assertion of the two.

## Why it is not already there

Two attempts, both blind, both removed:

1. **Per-row grep for the run of `b`s.** Cannot match by construction: the answer
   is what wraps, so the run is split across two rows and appears whole on
   neither. This one could never pass.
2. **Joining the rows back and grepping the joined text.** `restore_curline()`
   does exactly this to find the pair on screen, so it looked sound. It is not,
   at least not through `capture-pane`: with 62 `b`s typed at 72 columns, the two
   rows come back holding 10 and 46 of them. Those do not sum to 62 and do not
   concatenate to what was typed, so whatever `capture-pane` is doing to a
   wrapped line is not a straight row-by-row rendering.

Understanding (2) is probably a prerequisite for any fix, and may be interesting
in its own right — `restore_curline()` reads the window with `mvwinnstr()` rather
than through tmux, so the two are not obliged to agree, but a test that cannot
see what the code sees is worth knowing about.

## Fix sketch

Simplest robust form is a count over the whole screen against a baseline taken
before the answer is typed, since `b` occurs in the banner:

```sh
base=$(screen | tr -cd 'b' | wc -c)
# type the answer
after=$(screen | tr -cd 'b' | wc -c)
# expect after - base == 62
```

The baseline has to be retaken if the banner scrolls differently at the height
being tested. An answer made of a character that appears nowhere else on the
setup screen would avoid that entirely and is probably the better route — check
the banner first rather than assuming.

## Provenance

Raised by the `ui-review` sub-agent on the fix for #100, as a "consider"
rather than a defect. Filed after two blind attempts rather than shipping a
third guess; the block carries a comment pointing here.","createdAt":"2026-08-10T15:41:10Z","labels":[],"number":115,"title":"The wrapping-answer test asserts the question but not the answer","updatedAt":"2026-08-11T19:23:50Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/115"},{"assignees":[],"body":"`restore_curline()` in `tui.c` has two branches for placing the line it rebuilds.

The `oldmsgw > 0` branch — the terminal's width changed — anchors to the last row
with anything on it, and its comment explains why that matters:

> Anchored to the last row with anything on it, not to the bottom of the window.
> They are the same once the conversation has filled it, and different for the
> whole setup conversation and after every `clearscreen()` -- there the live line
> sits mid-window, and writing at the bottom left the stump above it with blank
> rows in between.

The `else` branch — width unchanged, so only the height moved — does not:

```c
wscrl(wmsg, 1);
wmove(wmsg, maxy - 1, 0);
```

The same argument applies to it. Where the conversation has not filled the
window, this puts the rebuilt line at the bottom with blank rows above it,
instead of directly under the conversation.

## Why it is not fixed already

It cannot be reached to be tested. Getting into that branch needs the pending
pair — the game's part-written line plus the answer being typed — to be longer
than the whole message window, since a pair that fits is found intact by the
search above and the branch is never entered. The longest pair the game can
produce is a prompt plus the 126-character input buffer, about 135 characters.
The smallest message window with two rows to scroll is wider than that.

So the defect is real by inspection and unreachable by construction, at least at
every terminal size the display accepts.

A fix would be the same expression the other branch uses, but it interacts with
the `wscrl()` on the line above — after a scroll the row that `last` named holds
different content — so it is not a copy-paste, and there is no way to observe
whether it is right.

## What would make it testable

Either a larger input buffer (`tui.c`'s own comment at the top of
`restore_curline()` says the 512/2048 buffers there want revisiting if the input
buffer grows), or a message window smaller than two rows of the longest pair,
which the geometry does not currently allow.

## Provenance

Raised by the `code-review` sub-agent while reviewing the fix for #100, as a
latent inconsistency it could not construct a live case for. Filed rather than
fixed there: changing untestable code on reasoning alone is what AGENTS.md step 4
argues against, and the branch is now commented to say so.","createdAt":"2026-08-10T05:12:08Z","labels":[],"number":114,"title":"restore_curline()'s height-only branch anchors to the bottom of the window","updatedAt":"2026-08-10T17:01:22Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/114"},{"assignees":[],"body":"`tests/instructions.sh` checks that `### Answering a finding` exists and that a
quoted pointer precedes it. It does not check that anything is *under* the
heading, so the section can be reduced to a stub and the suite stays green.

## How to see it

Gut the section to a few lines, keeping one sentence that contains the counted


## History

A floor of 850 characters against a body of about 1670 — roughly half — existed

## Fix sketch

Measure the body from the heading to the next `### ` or end of file, and fail
under a floor set at about half the real size. Roughly:

```sh
body=$(awk -v h='### ' -v n="$SECTION" '
    index($0, h n) == 1 { inb = 1; next }
    inb && index($0, h) == 1 { inb = 0 }
    inb { b += length($0) + 1 }
    END { print b + 0 }' "$AGENTS")
```

Guard the result for non-numeric output and a non-zero awk exit, the way the
`STANDARDS` count beside it already is. Set the floor deliberately, and note in
a comment that it needs re-aiming if the section grows a lot — a floor left far
under its section stops meaning anything, and nothing prompts a maintainer to

## Why it matters

This is the failure mode of a prose file that nothing compiles. A step that

## What exists today

`tests/instructions.sh` checks exactly one section, by name:


Adding a section and a pointer to it gets no coverage. Removing a section that
is not that one gets no coverage.

## Fix sketch

Collect the quoted strings that look like section references and check each has
a heading. The hard part is telling a pointer from an ordinary quotation —

The commit for #78 (`c2fd28b`) contains, on one line:

```
Filed, not fixed: #88 (shrinking under the panels' geometry and back
```

GitHub matched the substring `fixed: #88`, treated it as a closing
keyword, and closed #88 on merge — an issue the same sentence says is
*not* fixed, and which that change reproduced on its own merge-base. It
was reopened by hand.

## Why it will happen again

AGENTS.md step 9 asks every change to say which issues were filed, "in
the pull request body and in the summary of the work". Those lists sit
next to phrases like "filed, not fixed", "fixed in #x, not here", and
"this does not fix #y" — every one of which contains a closing keyword
followed by a reference. The workflow that requires the disclosure is
what creates the hazard, so it is worth handling rather than
remembering.

GitHub's keywords are `close`/`closes`/`closed`, `fix`/`fixes`/`fixed`,
`resolve`/`resolves`/`resolved`, each matched with an optional colon
before the reference and **without regard to the words in front of it**.

## Suggested approach

Cheapest is a wording convention plus something that checks it:

- Refer to issues that a change does *not* fix without a keyword
  anywhere before the number — "left open: #88", "see #88", "filed as
  #88". Reserve `Closes #n` for the issue the change actually closes,
  on a line of its own.
- Have the tests check it. `tests/instructions.sh` already reads files
  and asserts things about them; a check over `git log` on the branch
  for a keyword-plus-reference that is not on its own line would catch
  this before merge. That is where the "prove it can fail" work goes:
  break it by writing "not fixed: #1" in a scratch commit.

Worth also fixing the wording in `AGENTS.md` step 9 itself if it ends up
recommending a phrasing, so the guidance and the check agree.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A commit or PR body can name an unfixed issue without closing it.
- [ ] Something automated catches the mistake, and is proven able to
      fail.

`.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are
harness input, not prose: the YAML frontmatter is what lets the `Agent`
tool resolve a sub-agent, and the `description` field is what drives
auto-delegation. Nothing in the suite opens that directory.

`tests/instructions.sh` covers `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` only. So a
stray newline inside a `description`, a renamed `name`, a dropped closing
`---`, or a duplicated key would all ship green, and the first symptom
would be a pass that silently never runs.

That is the rule at `AGENTS.md` — "Confirm the harness actually loads
what you wrote. A definition in a directory the tool never reads is
inert, and from the outside it looks exactly like a step that was
carried out" — with no test behind it.

There is a second, softer half. #71 was filed because those `description`
fields had drifted from what `AGENTS.md` says about when each pass binds,
and fixing it was hand work against hand-read prose. The drift will
recur: the fields and the workflow steps are edited at different times
for different reasons.

## Suggested approach

Extend `tests/instructions.sh`, which already runs in CI:

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `.claude/agents/*.md` with broken or missing frontmatter fails

`tests/score.sh` (added with #62) holds every score-sheet format string
in `finish.c` to column 47. It works, and it reaches what no journey can
— ten of the twelve singular forms and four of the five skill labels
appear in no recording — but it does so by scraping C source text, and

  honouring those widths, only `golden` would notice.
- **It degrades under reformatting.** A literal split by C string

  twelve dual-form `proutf` lines are 118-122 columns, so "wrap the long
  lines" is a plausible future chore that trips it.

## Suggested approach

Hoist the literals into a table `score()` indexes:


test, or a new one — by `snprintf`-ing each entry with representative
arguments and checking the result is 47 columns.

real semantics instead of a model of them, is immune to how the source
is wrapped, and deletes the awk.

Raised by the `code-review` sub-agent while reviewing #62, which is where

[AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).","createdAt":"2026-08-07T01:41:25Z","labels":[{"id":"LA_kwDOGnGsxM7b9ZOD","name":"good first issue","description":"Good for newcomers","color":"7057ff"}],"number":76,"title":"Assert the score sheet's columns from the compiled game, not from its source text","updatedAt":"2026-08-07T01:41:25Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/76"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`tests/instructions.sh` guards `AGENTS.md` in only three ways: the file
exists, it is at least 2000 bytes, and it contains a
`## Development workflow` heading. Everything else in that test is aimed
at keeping `CLAUDE.md` a short pointer.

So nothing checks the workflow list itself. A duplicate or skipped step
number, or a cross-reference left pointing at the wrong step after a
renumbering, ships green.

This is not hypothetical. Adding the "file what you found" step
renumbered three steps, and the checks that caught the problems were all
done by hand: a duplicated `10.` marker, a `steps 6-8` note that had to
be re-read against the steps it names, and a clause citing "steps 7 and
8" for a rule that also covered step 6.

## Why it matters

The workflow is the one document every agent in this repository is
required to follow, and a step reference that points at the wrong step
misdirects silently -- the file still reads plausibly. It is also the
file most likely to be renumbered again, since every new rule inserted
mid-list shifts everything below it.

Extend `tests/instructions.sh`, which already runs in CI as the
`instructions` test:

- Assert the top-level ordered-list markers in the `## Development
  workflow` section run consecutively from 1 with no gaps or repeats.
- Assert every `step N` and `steps N-M` reference in `AGENTS.md` falls
  within that range.

Both are a few lines of `awk` or `sed` over the file, need no new tool,
and would have caught all three of the problems above.

Worth considering while there: markdown continuation indent for
two-digit markers (`10.` needs four spaces where `9.` needs three).
Getting that wrong silently breaks the list into two, which no check
would currently notice either.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A duplicated, skipped, or out-of-order workflow step number fails
      the `instructions` test.
- [ ] A `step N` reference outside the range of real steps fails it too.
- [ ] The test still passes on the current `AGENTS.md`.

[{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`.claude/agents/verifier.md` names the tests that report SKIPPED rather
than failing, and tells the `verifier` to report such a skip as an
environment gap rather than passing over it. It covers `tui` (needs

#187 adds a third with identical skip semantics: `workflow`, registered

when its shellcheck integration is inert. The brief says nothing about
it.

## Why it matters

`actionlint` is not a build dependency of a C game, so it is absent on a
normal developer machine — `README.md` now says outright that this is
the test you are most likely to see skip. A `verifier` on such a machine
reports "13/13 passed" with the workflow lint silently unrun, which is a
weaker claim than it reads as.

Bounded, not severe: Linux CI installs both tools and `tests/workflow.sh`
hard-fails there rather than skipping, so the coverage is not lost in the
place that gates a merge. What is lost is the local signal, and the
`verifier` is exactly the pass that is supposed to notice a check that

## Where it was found

By `code-review` on the branch for #187, as a nit. Filed rather than

`tests/workflow.sh` (added for #187) lints `.github/workflows/` with

`run:` body. What it cannot check — and the header of that file says so

## Why it matters

The macOS legs are the ones nobody can reproduce locally, so a missing

#187 suggested the cheap version, and it is probably right:

The design question is what the list is. `timeout` is the one the

Whatever it checks, it needs a mutation proof that it can fail — per

`tests/tui.sh`'s `slept_drag()` helper registers the process it stops in
`stopped_pid` so `finish()` can `SIGCONT` it, and explains why:

> Recorded so finish() can let it go again. tm kill-server hangs up the
> pane, and a SIGSTOPped process never acts on SIGHUP, so an interrupt
> inside this window would orphan the game still stopped -- silently,
> since the directory it played in is gone by then.

Measured on Linux, that does not happen. `tm kill-server` reaps the
stopped game every time:

| case | after `tm kill-server` |
| --- | --- |
| `kill -STOP` on a game in a `start()` pane | gone |
| real Ctrl-Z in a job-control pane, run 1 | gone |
| run 2 | gone |
| run 3 | gone |

The reason is POSIX's orphaned-process-group rule: when the session
leader exits and leaves a process group orphaned with a stopped member,
the kernel sends `SIGHUP` **followed by `SIGCONT`** to that group. The
stopped process is continued and then dies of the hangup. The comment's
premise -- "a SIGSTOPped process never acts on SIGHUP" -- is true in
isolation and beside the point, because the SIGCONT arrives with it.

## Why it matters

The guard itself is worth keeping: it costs a line, and this was
measured on one platform where the suite runs on two -- macOS may
genuinely differ, and nobody has checked. What is wrong is the stated
reason, which claims an observed hazard where there is an unobserved
one. `AGENTS.md` step 4 treats a comment's *why* as specification, and
this one would have a reader believe the guard is load-bearing on Linux
when it is insurance.

It also cost something concrete: on the branch for #158 I copied the
claim into two new suspend arms, reasoning from it rather than from a
measurement, and the verifier had to catch the same wrong sentence a
second time. A wrong reason propagates the way a wrong number does.

## Where it was found

By the `verifier` on the branch for #158, checking whether that branch's
two new `stopped_pid` registrations could interact with `slept_drag()`'s.

branch corrects the claim in its own two arms and cites this issue;
`slept_drag()` is on `main` and was left alone, per step 9.

## Fixing it

Say what is true: on Linux the orphaned-process-group rule reaps a
stopped member, so the registration is insurance against a platform that
does not -- macOS being the one that has not been checked. Or check
macOS and say which way it goes, at which point the guard either has a
real reason or can go.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T10:36:21Z","labels":[],"number":192,"title":"slept_drag()'s comment says tm kill-server cannot reap a stopped process; on Linux it does","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T10:36:21Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/192"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

Suspend a full-screen game, resize the terminal while it is stopped, and
resume it: the frame comes back with its right-hand edge unpainted.

Journey, measured:

Compare the rightmost column against the same journey with no resize
while stopped.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T05:55:04Z","labels":[],"number":191,"title":"A panels-up game resized while suspended comes back missing the status panel's right border","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T05:55:04Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/191"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

Suspend the game at `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` and resume it, and the
space bar does nothing: the player has to press Enter before paging
continues. The next pause behaves normally.

## Why

`getch()` in `osx.c` puts the terminal into non-canonical, no-echo mode
with `tcsetattr()` and then blocks in `read()`. A stop and continue
leaves the terminal in canonical mode -- the shell restores what it
saved when it took the foreground back -- while the reader is still
blocked in the read it set up before the stop. In canonical mode the
line discipline holds the space until a newline arrives, so the read
does not return until Enter.

## Reproduced

Both modes, side by side at 80x24:

- plain (`sst` with no `-t`)
- `-t` fallen back to the classic display

Both swallow the space and both take Enter instead, so this is not
specific to the full-screen path or to anything curses does. A `-t` game
whose panels are **up** is unaffected: `tui_getch()` reads through
curses, which reinstates its own program mode on resume.

## Why it matters

Small, and recoverable without knowing anything -- pressing Enter works,
and most players would press something else and move on. It is worth
filing because the manual promises resizing is safe "while the game
waits for an answer or for a keystroke at a pause" and this is the
neighbouring gesture failing quietly, and because the reader is one
`tcsetattr()` away from being right.

## Where it was found

By `ui-review` on the branch for #158, which fixed a *different* suspend
defect: a fallback game could not be resumed at all, because
`endwin()` left curses' `SIGTSTP` handler installed. That is fixed and
this is what is left. Explicitly not caused by it -- plain mode, which
that change does not touch, behaves identically -- so it was filed
rather than folded in.

## Fixing it

`getch()` could re-apply its own termios after the read returns EINTR,
or set the mode again immediately before each `read()` rather than once
before the loop. Worth checking against #150's `EINTR` retry, which is
the loop this would sit inside, and against `readinput()`, which reads
lines and wants canonical mode -- so it is only the keystroke reader
that needs this.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T05:27:56Z","labels":[],"number":190,"title":"A pause resumed after a suspend swallows the space bar and wants Enter instead","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T05:27:56Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/190"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`AGENTS.md:425`, in the "Who runs which tests" section, says:

> Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
> `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.

Measured repeatedly on this machine over the last two branches:

| run | configuration | wall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctest --preset ci-debug` | Debug | 377.8s / 378.4s / 379.8s |
| `ctest --preset ci-release` | Release | 368.3s / 368.7s / 370.7s |

That is **6m10s and 6m10s**, not four minutes — out by about 55%.

## Why it matters

The sentence is doing work, not decoration. It is the cost argument for
the whole main-agent/`verifier` split: it is why the main agent is told
not to pre-run the battery, and why a second full run is called a waste.
The argument gets *stronger* with the true number, so nothing built on
it is wrong — but the figure is the one a reader will quote when
deciding whether some new pass is affordable, and it is now the third
stale timing claim found in this repository, after `CMakeLists.txt`'s
"~11s" for the `tui` test (#101) and my own bad estimate in #101's
comments.

It also interacts with two open issues:

- **#101** — `tui` alone is 195s of that ~378s, and growing.
- **#186** — the CI job budget is 15 minutes, so a ~6-minute suite per
  configuration leaves much less slack for anything before it than a
  4-minute one implies. That is the arithmetic the install-step cap in
  #186 had to be sized against.

## Where it was found

By `code-review` on the branch for #186, which noticed the workflow
comment citing "about six minutes per configuration" and flagged that it
contradicted `AGENTS.md:425` — one of the two written numbers had to be
stale, and it is this one. Filed rather than fixed on that branch, per
step 9: the branch is a CI workflow change and `AGENTS.md` is not in its
diff.

## Fixing it

Replace the figure, and consider whether it should be a figure at all.
Three of these have now gone stale. Something like "a full `ctest` here
runs for minutes per configuration, most of it the `tui` test" carries
the argument without a number that has to be maintained — and where a
number is genuinely wanted, saying where and when it was measured is
what the repository asks of comments elsewhere.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T02:51:20Z","labels":[],"number":188,"title":"AGENTS.md says a full ctest is about four minutes per configuration; it is over six","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T02:51:20Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/188"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`sync_size()` calls `clearok(curscr, TRUE)` before re-laying-out, added
for #168 so a pinned axis whose window scrolled underneath it gets a
full repaint rather than a difference. Nothing tests that call on the
only ground where it is the sole repair.

`tests/tui.sh` has four arms that cover the repaint machinery -- "pin
drag", "pin fast drag", "pin slept drag", "pin slept pause". Remove all
three `clearok(curscr, TRUE)` calls and all four fail. Remove
`sync_size()`'s **alone** and the whole file stays green, because every
one of those arms has a reader waiting, so each resize also arrives as a
`KEY_RESIZE` and the two reader-level repaints heal it.

## Where it is the only repair

When `sync_size()` runs with no reader waiting to be handed a
`KEY_RESIZE` -- a resize landing while the game is *printing*. That is
the case `sync_size()`'s own comment has always been about:

> Called before every repaint rather than only where a resize is
> reported, because a drag can land while no reader is waiting --
> setting a quadrant up, printing a destruct countdown -- and the
> repaint would then be drawn to the old geometry.

## Why it is hard to test

The destruct countdown is the game's one long stretch of output with no
read in it, and it is not long. Measured on this branch's debug build,
from the `SELF-DESTRUCT-SEQUENCE-ACTIVATED` line to the last digit:
**under one second**, end to end. A shell-driven arm cannot reliably
land a `resize-window` inside that, and the countdown ends the game, so
an arm that misses the window asserts against a screen with no panels
on it.

## Why it matters

`sync_size()`'s call is kept on the strength of a code path rather than
of a test, which is stated plainly in the comment beside it and in the
"pin drag" arm. That is honest but fragile: someone tidying up the three
`clearok` calls would find the suite green after deleting this one, and
nothing would tell them what they had removed.

## Where it was found

While re-proving the #168 arms after adding the reader-level repaints:
a mutation that used to fail "pin drag" stopped failing it, because the
later fix healed the same case by another route. The proof note in that
arm was corrected at the same time -- it had become a true statement
about a build that no longer exists.

## Fixing it

Options, roughly in order of appeal:

- Slow the countdown under a test-only hook, or find another
  output-without-read stretch long enough to drag across.
- Drive it from a harness that can resize at a known point --
  `openpty` + `TIOCSWINSZ` from Python gives byte-level control of when
  the SIGWINCH lands, which shell plus tmux does not. That is a new
  dependency for a suite that is sh-only and also runs on macOS CI, so
  it is a real cost.
- Accept it as untestable and say so where the call is, which is what
  the branch does today.","createdAt":"2026-08-19T05:31:58Z","labels":[],"number":184,"title":"sync_size()'s repaint has no test on its own ground: a resize while the game is printing","updatedAt":"2026-08-19T06:14:48Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/184"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

Three functions in `tui.c` each spell out the same ioctl and the same
zero guard:

```c
ioctl(fileno(stdout), TIOCGWINSZ, &ws) != 0 || ws.ws_row <= 0 || ws.ws_col <= 0
```

- `term_size()` — added for #168, and now the natural home for it
- `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()`
- `tui_init()`

All three carry a comment explaining the same case: an ioctl can succeed
and report 0x0, which is what `openpty()` gives you until somebody sets a
winsize, and reading that as a size is wrong. Three copies of the rule,
three copies of the explanation.

## Why it matters

The file already argues against this shape, about a smaller duplication
than this one. From `blames()`:

> Named rather than repeated there, so a change to either half cannot
> reach one caller and not the other.

That is the risk here. The guard has already been sharpened once, on the
#168 branch, when a `verifier` finding showed the case it actually earns
is the *half*-zero winsize (rows set, columns not) rather than the whole
-zero one the comments named — a whole-zero answer is caught downstream
by `layo…23456 tokens truncated…lready reads files
  and asserts things about them; a check over `git log` on the branch
  for a keyword-plus-reference that is not on its own line would catch
  this before merge. That is where the "prove it can fail" work goes:
  break it by writing "not fixed: #1" in a scratch commit.

Worth also fixing the wording in `AGENTS.md` step 9 itself if it ends up
recommending a phrasing, so the guidance and the check agree.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A commit or PR body can name an unfixed issue without closing it.
- [ ] Something automated catches the mistake, and is proven able to
      fail.

Found while merging #92; #88 was the casualty. Follow the workflow in
[AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).","createdAt":"2026-08-08T07:36:54Z","labels":[],"number":93,"title":"A commit body that names an issue can close it by accident","updatedAt":"2026-08-08T07:36:54Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/93"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Gap

`tests/test_tuifmt.c` checks that `fmt_status_line()` mirrors `srscan()`,
but never checks how wide its output is. The widest line the game can
produce is `Shields       DAMAGED, 100% 2500.0 units` at 40 columns,
against exactly 40 columns of room in the status panel at the 72-column
minimum — `COLS - QUADW` less the two borders and the two-column indent.

Zero slack, and nothing asserts it.

## Why it matters

Before #78 an over-long line wrapped onto the next row and wrecked the

`.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are
harness input, not prose: the YAML frontmatter is what lets the `Agent`
tool resolve a sub-agent, and the `description` field is what drives
auto-delegation. Nothing in the suite opens that directory.

`tests/instructions.sh` covers `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` only. So a
stray newline inside a `description`, a renamed `name`, a dropped closing
`---`, or a duplicated key would all ship green, and the first symptom
would be a pass that silently never runs.

That is the rule at `AGENTS.md` — "Confirm the harness actually loads
what you wrote. A definition in a directory the tool never reads is
inert, and from the outside it looks exactly like a step that was
carried out" — with no test behind it.

There is a second, softer half. #71 was filed because those `description`
fields had drifted from what `AGENTS.md` says about when each pass binds,
and fixing it was hand work against hand-read prose. The drift will
recur: the fields and the workflow steps are edited at different times
for different reasons.

## Suggested approach

Extend `tests/instructions.sh`, which already runs in CI:

- For each file in `.claude/agents/`, assert the frontmatter opens and
  closes, parses, carries exactly `name`, `description` and `tools`, and
  that `name` matches the filename. No YAML parser is needed for that —
  the fields are one line each by construction, which is itself the
  property worth asserting.
- Assert each `description` is a single line, since that is the failure
  that breaks loading without looking broken.
- Assert the three names the workflow invokes (`ui-review`, `verifier`,
  `code-review`) all exist, so deleting one is a failure rather than a
  silent skip.

The agreement half is harder and probably not worth automating: whether a
`description` matches what step 6 says cannot be checked by grep without
encoding the prose twice. Worth deciding rather than assuming — a cheap
approximation is to assert each description mentions the pass it must
follow, which would have caught `verifier.md` claiming to run after a
`ui-review` that may not have run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `.claude/agents/*.md` with broken or missing frontmatter fails
      the `instructions` test.
- [ ] A `description` split across two lines fails it.
- [ ] Removing one of the three definitions fails it.

`tests/score.sh` (added with #62) holds every score-sheet format string
in `finish.c` to column 47. It works, and it reaches what no journey can
— ten of the twelve singular forms and four of the five skill labels
appear in no recording — but it does so by scraping C source text, and

  honouring those widths, only `golden` would notice.
- **It degrades under reformatting.** A literal split by C string

  twelve dual-form `proutf` lines are 118-122 columns, so "wrap the long
  lines" is a plausible future chore that trips it.

Hoist the literals into a table `score()` indexes:


Then assert in C — `tests/test_rules.c` is the existing home for a C
test, or a new one — by `snprintf`-ing each entry with representative
arguments and checking the result is 47 columns.

That reaches every singular form and every skill label, uses printf's
real semantics instead of a model of them, is immune to how the source
is wrapped, and deletes the awk.

Worth deciding while there what to do about the two lines the table
cannot hold as single formats: the winning bonus, assembled from a
prefix, a skill label and a tail, and the `Penalty for getting yourself
killed` literal, which carries no conversion at all.

      prints, not against the text of `finish.c`.
- [ ] Every singular and plural form is still covered, and the skill
      labels with them.
- [ ] `tests/score.sh` is deleted, or reduced to whatever the C test
      cannot reach, and `CMakeLists.txt` updated to match.

`tests/instructions.sh` guards `AGENTS.md` in only three ways: the file
exists, it is at least 2000 bytes, and it contains a
`## Development workflow` heading. Everything else in that test is aimed
at keeping `CLAUDE.md` a short pointer.

So nothing checks the workflow list itself. A duplicate or skipped step
number, or a cross-reference left pointing at the wrong step after a
renumbering, ships green.

This is not hypothetical. Adding the "file what you found" step
renumbered three steps, and the checks that caught the problems were all
done by hand: a duplicated `10.` marker, a `steps 6-8` note that had to
be re-read against the steps it names, and a clause citing "steps 7 and
8" for a rule that also covered step 6.

## Why it matters

The workflow is the one document every agent in this repository is
required to follow, and a step reference that points at the wrong step
misdirects silently -- the file still reads plausibly. It is also the
file most likely to be renumbered again, since every new rule inserted
mid-list shifts everything below it.

## Suggested approach

Extend `tests/instructions.sh`, which already runs in CI as the
`instructions` test:

- Assert the top-level ordered-list markers in the `## Development
  workflow` section run consecutively from 1 with no gaps or repeats.
- Assert every `step N` and `steps N-M` reference in `AGENTS.md` falls
  within that range.

Both are a few lines of `awk` or `sed` over the file, need no new tool,
and would have caught all three of the problems above.

Worth considering while there: markdown continuation indent for
two-digit markers (`10.` needs four spaces where `9.` needs three).
Getting that wrong silently breaks the list into two, which no check
would currently notice either.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A duplicated, skipped, or out-of-order workflow step number fails
      the `instructions` test.
- [ ] A `step N` reference outside the range of real steps fails it too.
- [ ] The test still passes on the current `AGENTS.md`.

`tests/tui.sh`'s `slept_drag()` helper registers the process it stops in
`stopped_pid` so `finish()` can `SIGCONT` it, and explains why:

> Recorded so finish() can let it go again. tm kill-server hangs up the
> pane, and a SIGSTOPped process never acts on SIGHUP, so an interrupt
> inside this window would orphan the game still stopped -- silently,
> since the directory it played in is gone by then.

Measured on Linux, that does not happen. `tm kill-server` reaps the
stopped game every time:

| case | after `tm kill-server` |
| --- | --- |
| `kill -STOP` on a game in a `start()` pane | gone |
| real Ctrl-Z in a job-control pane, run 1 | gone |
| run 2 | gone |
| run 3 | gone |

The reason is POSIX's orphaned-process-group rule: when the session
leader exits and leaves a process group orphaned with a stopped member,
the kernel sends `SIGHUP` **followed by `SIGCONT`** to that group. The
stopped process is continued and then dies of the hangup. The comment's
premise -- "a SIGSTOPped process never acts on SIGHUP" -- is true in
isolation and beside the point, because the SIGCONT arrives with it.

## Why it matters

The guard itself is worth keeping: it costs a line, and this was
measured on one platform where the suite runs on two -- macOS may
genuinely differ, and nobody has checked. What is wrong is the stated
reason, which claims an observed hazard where there is an unobserved
one. `AGENTS.md` step 4 treats a comment's *why* as specification, and
this one would have a reader believe the guard is load-bearing on Linux
when it is insurance.

It also cost something concrete: on the branch for #158 I copied the
claim into two new suspend arms, reasoning from it rather than from a
measurement, and the verifier had to catch the same wrong sentence a
second time. A wrong reason propagates the way a wrong number does.

## Where it was found

By the `verifier` on the branch for #158, checking whether that branch's
two new `stopped_pid` registrations could interact with `slept_drag()`'s.
They cannot -- but the shared premise turned out not to hold. The #158
branch corrects the claim in its own two arms and cites this issue;
`slept_drag()` is on `main` and was left alone, per step 9.

stopped member, so the registration is insurance against a platform that
does not -- macOS being the one that has not been checked. Or check
macOS and say which way it goes, at which point the guard either has a
real reason or can go.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T10:36:21Z","labels":[],"number":192,"title":"slept_drag()'s comment says tm kill-server cannot reap a stopped process; on Linux it does","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T10:36:21Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/192"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

Suspend a full-screen game, resize the terminal while it is stopped, and
resume it: the frame comes back with its right-hand edge unpainted.

Journey, measured:

1. `sst -t` at 100x30, panels up, at `COMMAND>`
2. `Ctrl-Z`
3. resize the terminal to 90x26 **while the game is stopped**
4. `fg`

The top and bottom rules are redrawn to the new width but lose their
corner characters, and every interior row of the Status panel ends
without its border -- the whole rightmost screen column is unpainted.
The next output repaints it and the frame is whole again.

## Why it matters

Cosmetic and self-healing: one keystroke puts it right, and nothing is
lost. It is worth filing because it is a visible frame defect on a
gesture that is otherwise well covered -- the resize path has had a lot
of work (#163, #164, #166, #168) and both manuals promise the panels
follow the terminal -- and because a player who sees it has no way to
know it will heal.

The likely shape: curses' SIGTSTP handler does its own `reset_prog_mode()`
and refresh on resume, from a screen size it recorded before the stop,
and the resize that happened in between is applied to some of the frame
and not all of it. That is a guess from the symptom, not a measurement.

## Scope: pre-existing, and not caused by #158

Reproduced identically on a build of `main`, on the **first-init** path
(a game that came up full-screen straight away), which the #158 branch
does not touch.

That branch does make it reachable on one more path -- a game that fell
back, then came up full-screen at the play-again retry -- but only
because it restores curses' suspend handling there, which is the whole
point of the change: the retry path now behaves like the first-init one,
including in this.

## Where it was found

By `ui-review` on the branch for #158, while checking that the retry and
first-init suspend paths had been made consistent with each other. They
have; this is what they are consistently doing.

## How to see it

In a real terminal, or tmux:

Suspend the game at `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` and resume it, and the
space bar does nothing: the player has to press Enter before paging
continues. The next pause behaves normally.

## Why

`getch()` in `osx.c` puts the terminal into non-canonical, no-echo mode
with `tcsetattr()` and then blocks in `read()`. A stop and continue
leaves the terminal in canonical mode -- the shell restores what it
saved when it took the foreground back -- while the reader is still
blocked in the read it set up before the stop. In canonical mode the
line discipline holds the space until a newline arrives, so the read
does not return until Enter.

## Reproduced

Both modes, side by side at 80x24:

- plain (`sst` with no `-t`)
- `-t` fallen back to the classic display

Both swallow the space and both take Enter instead, so this is not
specific to the full-screen path or to anything curses does. A `-t` game
whose panels are **up** is unaffected: `tui_getch()` reads through
curses, which reinstates its own program mode on resume.

## Why it matters

Small, and recoverable without knowing anything -- pressing Enter works,
and most players would press something else and move on. It is worth
filing because the manual promises resizing is safe "while the game
waits for an answer or for a keystroke at a pause" and this is the
neighbouring gesture failing quietly, and because the reader is one
`tcsetattr()` away from being right.

## Where it was found

By `ui-review` on the branch for #158, which fixed a *different* suspend
defect: a fallback game could not be resumed at all, because
`endwin()` left curses' `SIGTSTP` handler installed. That is fixed and
this is what is left. Explicitly not caused by it -- plain mode, which
that change does not touch, behaves identically -- so it was filed
rather than folded in.

## Fixing it

`getch()` could re-apply its own termios after the read returns EINTR,
or set the mode again immediately before each `read()` rather than once
before the loop. Worth checking against #150's `EINTR` retry, which is
the loop this would sit inside, and against `readinput()`, which reads
lines and wants canonical mode -- so it is only the keystroke reader
that needs this.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T05:27:56Z","labels":[],"number":190,"title":"A pause resumed after a suspend swallows the space bar and wants Enter instead","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T05:27:56Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/190"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`AGENTS.md:425`, in the "Who runs which tests" section, says:

> Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
> `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.

Measured repeatedly on this machine over the last two branches:

| run | configuration | wall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctest --preset ci-debug` | Debug | 377.8s / 378.4s / 379.8s |
| `ctest --preset ci-release` | Release | 368.3s / 368.7s / 370.7s |

That is **6m10s and 6m10s**, not four minutes — out by about 55%.

## Why it matters

The sentence is doing work, not decoration. It is the cost argument for
the whole main-agent/`verifier` split: it is why the main agent is told
not to pre-run the battery, and why a second full run is called a waste.
The argument gets *stronger* with the true number, so nothing built on
it is wrong — but the figure is the one a reader will quote when
deciding whether some new pass is affordable, and it is now the third
stale timing claim found in this repository, after `CMakeLists.txt`'s
"~11s" for the `tui` test (#101) and my own bad estimate in #101's
comments.

It also interacts with two open issues:

- **#101** — `tui` alone is 195s of that ~378s, and growing.
- **#186** — the CI job budget is 15 minutes, so a ~6-minute suite per
  configuration leaves much less slack for anything before it than a
  4-minute one implies. That is the arithmetic the install-step cap in
  #186 had to be sized against.

## Where it was found

By `code-review` on the branch for #186, which noticed the workflow
comment citing "about six minutes per configuration" and flagged that it
contradicted `AGENTS.md:425` — one of the two written numbers had to be
stale, and it is this one. Filed rather than fixed on that branch, per
step 9: the branch is a CI workflow change and `AGENTS.md` is not in its
diff.

## Fixing it

Replace the figure, and consider whether it should be a figure at all.
Three of these have now gone stale. Something like "a full `ctest` here
runs for minutes per configuration, most of it the `tui` test" carries
the argument without a number that has to be maintained — and where a
number is genuinely wanted, saying where and when it was measured is
what the repository asks of comments elsewhere.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T02:51:20Z","labels":[],"number":188,"title":"AGENTS.md says a full ctest is about four minutes per configuration; it is over six","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T02:51:20Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/188"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`sync_size()` calls `clearok(curscr, TRUE)` before re-laying-out, added
for #168 so a pinned axis whose window scrolled underneath it gets a
full repaint rather than a difference. Nothing tests that call on the
only ground where it is the sole repair.

`tests/tui.sh` has four arms that cover the repaint machinery -- "pin
drag", "pin fast drag", "pin slept drag", "pin slept pause". Remove all
three `clearok(curscr, TRUE)` calls and all four fail. Remove
`sync_size()`'s **alone** and the whole file stays green, because every
one of those arms has a reader waiting, so each resize also arrives as a
`KEY_RESIZE` and the two reader-level repaints heal it.

## Where it is the only repair

When `sync_size()` runs with no reader waiting to be handed a
`KEY_RESIZE` -- a resize landing while the game is *printing*. That is
the case `sync_size()`'s own comment has always been about:

> Called before every repaint rather than only where a resize is
> reported, because a drag can land while no reader is waiting --
> setting a quadrant up, printing a destruct countdown -- and the
> repaint would then be drawn to the old geometry.

## Why it is hard to test

The destruct countdown is the game's one long stretch of output with no
read in it, and it is not long. Measured on this branch's debug build,
from the `SELF-DESTRUCT-SEQUENCE-ACTIVATED` line to the last digit:
**under one second**, end to end. A shell-driven arm cannot reliably
land a `resize-window` inside that, and the countdown ends the game, so
an arm that misses the window asserts against a screen with no panels
on it.

## Why it matters

`sync_size()`'s call is kept on the strength of a code path rather than
of a test, which is stated plainly in the comment beside it and in the
"pin drag" arm. That is honest but fragile: someone tidying up the three
`clearok` calls would find the suite green after deleting this one, and
nothing would tell them what they had removed.

## Where it was found

While re-proving the #168 arms after adding the reader-level repaints:
a mutation that used to fail "pin drag" stopped failing it, because the
later fix healed the same case by another route. The proof note in that
arm was corrected at the same time -- it had become a true statement
about a build that no longer exists.

## Fixing it

Options, roughly in order of appeal:

- Slow the countdown under a test-only hook, or find another
  output-without-read stretch long enough to drag across.
- Drive it from a harness that can resize at a known point --
  `openpty` + `TIOCSWINSZ` from Python gives byte-level control of when
  the SIGWINCH lands, which shell plus tmux does not. That is a new
  dependency for a suite that is sh-only and also runs on macOS CI, so
  it is a real cost.
- Accept it as untestable and say so where the call is, which is what
  the branch does today.","createdAt":"2026-08-19T05:31:58Z","labels":[],"number":184,"title":"sync_size()'s repaint has no test on its own ground: a resize while the game is printing","updatedAt":"2026-08-19T06:14:48Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/184"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

Three functions in `tui.c` each spell out the same ioctl and the same
zero guard:

```c
ioctl(fileno(stdout), TIOCGWINSZ, &ws) != 0 || ws.ws_row <= 0 || ws.ws_col <= 0
```

- `term_size()` — added for #168, and now the natural home for it
- `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()`
- `tui_init()`

All three carry a comment explaining the same case: an ioctl can succeed
and report 0x0, which is what `openpty()` gives you until somebody sets a
winsize, and reading that as a size is wrong. Three copies of the rule,
three copies of the explanation.

## Why it matters

The file already argues against this shape, about a smaller duplication
than this one. From `blames()`:

> Named rather than repeated there, so a change to either half cannot
> reach one caller and not the other.

That is the risk here. The guard has already been sharpened once, on the
#168…6838 tokens truncated…

#82 put a clause on `code-review.md`'s pointer into `AGENTS.md`: read the
section from the repository, not from a copy already in context. It also
gave `verifier.md` a paragraph covering *any* file a check reads — the
manual, a test, a source file a comment cites.

`code-review.md` did not get the general form, and it has the same
exposure. Its own instructions send the reviewer to `sst.doc` twice —
"behavior that contradicts `sst.doc`" (`.claude/agents/code-review.md:26`)

(`:39-40`) — and to `sst.h` and callers at `:20-21`. A sub-agent
typically meets those files as excerpts quoted into its task description
from the main agent's memory of them, which is exactly the route
`verifier.md` now warns about, and the work under review may have changed
them since.

## Why it was left out of #82

Deliberately, and the reason is worth keeping. #82's second acceptance
criterion is that the two definitions it names say it the same way, and
`ui-review.md` and `code-review.md` currently satisfy it byte for byte.
Broadening one of them would have broken that parity inside the slice
that established it. So the narrow clause shipped and this was split off
rather than folded in.

## What to decide

Not "add the paragraph to `code-review.md`" — that recreates the parity
problem. The question is whether the general rule should be stated once
in a place all three definitions reach, with each keeping only a short
pointer to it. That is the shape #82's own "Suggested approach" raised
and did not settle, and it has to survive the constraint that started all
this: the rule cannot live only in `AGENTS.md`, because the copy of

definition can be the stale copy too, so "put it in the definitions" is
not automatically safe either.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `code-review` sub-agent handed a quoted `sst.doc` excerpt is told

- [ ] Whatever shape it takes does not regress #82's parity criterion.

Two sub-agent sessions on #82 were asked to compare their own injected
context against the repository. They came out opposite ways, on the same
branch, hours apart:

| | injected `AGENTS.md` | injected own definition | injected `gitStatus` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `verifier`, round 1 | stale (`be17114`, 15 commits back) | current | not checked |
| `code-review`, round 2 | stale (`be17114`) | current (contained #80's text) | stale: branch `main`, tip `be17114`, date three days off |
| `verifier`, round 4 | **current** (HEAD) | **stale** — byte-identical to `HEAD:.claude/agents/verifier.md`, missing the paragraph in the working tree it had been asked to verify | not checked |

The last row is the one that matters. #82's fix rests on the assumption
that a sub-agent's own definition is loaded fresh at invocation while
`AGENTS.md` is a session-start snapshot — that asymmetry is *why* the
clause was put in the definitions rather than in `AGENTS.md`. Round 4
shows the asymmetry does not hold in both directions: a definition is a
snapshot too, and it can be the stale one while `AGENTS.md` is current.

The fix still works — it is strictly better than nothing under either
mechanism, and a definition that is merely behind `HEAD` still carries
whatever rule was last committed. But the repository should not go on
believing the mechanism is what it is not.

## Two distinct gaps

**1. `gitStatus` can name the wrong branch.** A reviewer was told
`Current branch: main`, tip `be17114`, while the worktree was on
`docs/pointers-read-from-the-repo` three days later. It caught this only
because it was explicitly asked to measure its context. An agent that
trusts that block inspects the wrong branch and reports on the wrong
diff — and unlike a stale file, there is no fresher copy to be pointed
at, only `git` itself. None of the three definitions currently says to
re-derive branch and tip from `git` rather than reading the block.

**2. A definition can be stale.** Nothing follows from this for the
definition's own rules, but it does mean an uncommitted change to a
sub-agent's instructions is invisible to that sub-agent — including,
as in round 4, while it is verifying that very change. Worth knowing
before someone tries to test an agent definition by editing it and
invoking it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The definitions tell an agent to take branch and tip from `git`,
      not from the injected status block. One sentence, in the same
      shape as #82's clause.
- [ ] Somewhere durable records that a definition is also a snapshot, so
      the next person reasoning about #82's design does not repeat the
      assumption that only `AGENTS.md` goes stale.

in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).","createdAt":"2026-08-08T02:20:04Z","labels":[],"number":85,"title":"The parts of a session's injected context go stale independently of each other","updatedAt":"2026-08-08T02:24:29Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/85"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`.claude/agents/ui-review.md`'s frontmatter `description` says:

> See "The review sub-agents" in AGENTS.md for when this binds; when it
> is unclear, run it.

Every other pointer into `AGENTS.md` now carries the clause added for
#82 — read it from the file in the repository, not from a copy already in
context. That one does not, and it is the one place the clause would not
help.

A `description` is read by the **main** agent, at the moment it decides
whether to delegate. That is the agent whose `AGENTS.md` is the stale
copy: both sub-agents that examined their own context on #82 found a
snapshot nine commits and three days behind the file on disk, with no
"The review sub-agents" section in it at all. Telling that reader to go
and read the section does not help if it does not know it is holding an
old copy, and unlike a sub-agent it is not starting a fresh context it
could be redirected to.

## Why it matters, and why it is not urgent

The practical backstop is already in place: `code-review` re-reads the
section from the repository and is required to dispute a
mis-classification, so a `ui-review` wrongly skipped on a player-visible
change should still be caught before the commit. What is missing is the
argument being written down anywhere — the reason the clause belongs in
`code-review.md` most of all is that it is the backstop for a decision
the main agent may have made from stale text.

## Suggested approach

Worth deciding rather than patching:

- Have the main agent re-read the section from the repository before
  deciding a skip, and say so in `AGENTS.md` step 6 — where the reader
  with the stale copy would have to notice a rule it may not have.
- Or accept that the decision can be made from an old copy and lean on
  `code-review` as the check, and say *that* in
  `.claude/agents/code-review.md` so the role is deliberate rather than
  incidental.

The second is closer to how it already works. The first is only worth it
if a skipped `ui-review` is judged too expensive to catch one pass later.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The repository says which of the two it relies on.
- [ ] If it is the second, `code-review.md` says that disputing a skip
      decided from stale text is part of the job.

`.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are
harness input, not prose: the YAML frontmatter is what lets the `Agent`
tool resolve a sub-agent, and the `description` field is what drives
auto-delegation. Nothing in the suite opens that directory.

`tests/instructions.sh` covers `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` only. So a
stray newline inside a `description`, a renamed `name`, a dropped closing
`---`, or a duplicated key would all ship green, and the first symptom
would be a pass that silently never runs.

That is the rule at `AGENTS.md` — "Confirm the harness actually loads
what you wrote. A definition in a directory the tool never reads is
inert, and from the outside it looks exactly like a step that was
carried out" — with no test behind it.

There is a second, softer half. #71 was filed because those `description`
fields had drifted from what `AGENTS.md` says about when each pass binds,
and fixing it was hand work against hand-read prose. The drift will
recur: the fields and the workflow steps are edited at different times
for different reasons.

## Suggested approach

Extend `tests/instructions.sh`, which already runs in CI:

- For each file in `.claude/agents/`, assert the frontmatter opens and
  closes, parses, carries exactly `name`, `description` and `tools`, and
  that `name` matches the filename. No YAML parser is needed for that —
  the fields are one line each by construction, which is itself the
  property worth asserting.
- Assert each `description` is a single line, since that is the failure
  that breaks loading without looking broken.
- Assert the three names the workflow invokes (`ui-review`, `verifier`,
  `code-review`) all exist, so deleting one is a failure rather than a
  silent skip.

The agreement half is harder and probably not worth automating: whether a
`description` matches what step 6 says cannot be checked by grep without
encoding the prose twice. Worth deciding rather than assuming — a cheap
approximation is to assert each description mentions the pass it must
follow, which would have caught `verifier.md` claiming to run after a
`ui-review` that may not have run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `.claude/agents/*.md` with broken or missing frontmatter fails
      the `instructions` test.
- [ ] A `description` split across two lines fails it.
- [ ] Removing one of the three definitions fails it.

`tests/score.sh` (added with #62) holds every score-sheet format string
in `finish.c` to column 47. It works, and it reaches what no journey can
— ten of the twelve singular forms and four of the five skill labels
appear in no recording — but it does so by scraping C source text, and
its own header admits the two costs:

- **It never sees the compiled game.** It re-implements printf width
  semantics in awk (`%6d` → 6, `%6.2f` → 6). If `proutf` ever stopped
  honouring those widths, only `golden` would notice.
- **It degrades under reformatting.** A literal split by C string
  concatenation drops out of the scan. That was a live false pass during
  review — a floor of 24 let it through silently — and it is now guarded
  by an exact count of 27, which is a tripwire rather than a fix. The
  twelve dual-form `proutf` lines are 118-122 columns, so "wrap the long
  lines" is a plausible future chore that trips it.

## Suggested approach

Hoist the literals into a table `score()` indexes:

```c
static const char *const score_lines[] = { ... };
```

Then assert in C — `tests/test_rules.c` is the existing home for a C
test, or a new one — by `snprintf`-ing each entry with representative
arguments and checking the result is 47 columns.

That reaches every singular form and every skill label, uses printf's
real semantics instead of a model of them, is immune to how the source
is wrapped, and deletes the awk.

Worth deciding while there what to do about the two lines the table
cannot hold as single formats: the winning bonus, assembled from a
prefix, a skill label and a tail, and the `Penalty for getting yourself
killed` literal, which carries no conversion at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The column invariant is asserted against what the compiled game
      prints, not against the text of `finish.c`.
- [ ] Every singular and plural form is still covered, and the skill
      labels with them.
- [ ] `tests/score.sh` is deleted, or reduced to whatever the C test
      cannot reach, and `CMakeLists.txt` updated to match.

Raised by the `code-review` sub-agent while reviewing #62, which is where
the scraping test came from. Follow the workflow in
[AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).","createdAt":"2026-08-07T01:41:25Z","labels":[{"id":"LA_kwDOGnGsxM7b9ZOD","name":"good first issue","description":"Good for newcomers","color":"7057ff"}],"number":76,"title":"Assert the score sheet's columns from the compiled game, not from its source text","updatedAt":"2026-08-07T01:41:25Z","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/76"},{"assignees":[],"body":"## Problem

`tests/instructions.sh` guards `AGENTS.md` in only three ways: the file
exists, it is at least 2000 bytes, and it contains a
`## Development workflow` heading. Everything else in that test is aimed
at keeping `CLAUDE.md` a short pointer.

So nothing checks the workflow list itself. A duplicate or skipped step
number, or a cross-reference left pointing at the wrong step after a
renumbering, ships green.

This is not hypothetical. Adding the "file what you found" step
renumbered three steps, and the checks that caught the problems were all
done by hand: a duplicated `10.` marker, a `steps 6-8` note that had to
be re-read against the steps it names, and a clause citing "steps 7 and
8" for a rule that also covered step 6.

## Why it matters

The workflow is the one document every agent in this repository is
required to follow, and a step reference that points at the wrong step
misdirects silently -- the file still reads plausibly. It is also the
file most likely to be renumbered again, since every new rule inserted
mid-list shifts everything below it.

## Suggested approach

Extend `tests/instructions.sh`, which already runs in CI as the
`instructions` test:

- Assert the top-level ordered-list markers in the `## Development
  workflow` section run consecutively from 1 with no gaps or repeats.
- Assert every `step N` and `steps N-M` reference in `AGENTS.md` falls
  within that range.

Both are a few lines of `awk` or `sed` over the file, need no new tool,
and would have caught all three of the problems above.

Worth considering while there: markdown continuation indent for
two-digit markers (`10.` needs four spaces where `9.` needs three).
Getting that wrong silently breaks the list into two, which no check
would currently notice either.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A duplicated, skipped, or out-of-order workflow step number fails
      the `instructions` test.
- [ ] A `step N` reference outside the range of real steps fails it too.
- [ ] The test still passes on the current `AGENTS.md`.

Found while adding the workflow step that requires findings like this
one to be filed. {"body":"## Problem

Three functions in `tui.c` each spell out the same ioctl and the same
zero guard:

```c
ioctl(fileno(stdout), TIOCGWINSZ, &ws) != 0 || ws.ws_row <= 0 || ws.ws_col <= 0
```

- `term_size()` — added for #168, and now the natural home for it
- `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()`
- `tui_init()`

All three carry a comment explaining the same case: an ioctl can succeed
and report 0x0, which is what `openpty()` gives you until somebody sets a
winsize, and reading that as a size is wrong. Three copies of the rule,
three copies of the explanation.

## Why it matters

The file already argues against this shape, about a smaller duplication
than this one. From `blames()`:

> Named rather than repeated there, so a change to either half cannot
> reach one caller and not the other.

That is the risk here. The guard has already been sharpened once, on the
#168 branch, when a `verifier` finding showed the case it actually earns
is the *half*-zero winsize (rows set, columns not) rather than the whole
-zero one the comments named — a whole-zero answer is caught downstream
by `layout_size()` anyway. Measured on a pty with `TIOCSWINSZ` at
rows=24, cols=0: with the guard the game reaches its command prompt
(2524 bytes of output), without it the layout is clipped to no columns
and it never gets there (3609 bytes, no `COMMAND`). That correction was
made in one comment. The other two still describe the case that cannot
reach them.

So the drift has already started, and it is the quiet kind: the code is
right in all three places and the reason given is wrong in two.

## Where it was found

By `code-review` on the branch for #168, which introduced the third
copy. Filed rather than fixed there because the other two call sites
belong to the startup-refusal machinery — `tui_init()`'s gate and the
notice `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()` feeds — which #168 does not
touch, and folding them in would put an unrelated refactor inside a diff
about the resize path. That is the split AGENTS.md step 9 asks for.

## Fixing it

`term_size()` is already the shape both other sites want:

```c
static void term_size(int *rows, int *cols);   /* zeros where the ioctl gave nothing */
```

Each existing site reduces to `term_size(&r, &c); if (r == 0) ...`, with
no behaviour change — the tests to lean on are the pinned arms in
`tests/tui.sh` ("pin shrink", "pin pending", "pin drag", "pin fast
drag") and the refusal arms ("oversize COLUMNS", "env size", "pinned
axis", "pinned height"). Move the explanation to `term_size()` and leave
each caller saying only what it does with a zero.

Worth checking while there: `term_size()` is declared above its callers
in file order, so no forward declaration is needed, but
`tui_size_changed_since_refusal()` and `tui_init()` sit far below it.","comments":[],"labels":[],"number":183,"title":"Three sites spell out the TIOCGWINSZ zero guard, and tui.c argues against exactly that","url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/183"}
